etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English beste, best, from Old English betst, betest, from Proto-Germanic *batistaz.

definitions.definition: superlative form of good: most good.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii], page 163, column 1:
quote.text: […]  when he is beſt, he is a little worſe then a man, and when he is worſt, he is little better than a beaſt:

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book V”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC, line 19:
quote.text: Heav'ns laſt beſt gift, my ever new delight,

quote.citation: 2011 October 7, Lana Del Rey, Justin Parker (lyrics and music), “Video Games”, in Born to Die, performed by Lana Del Rey:
quote.text: Swinging in the backyard  Pull up in your fast car whistling my name  Open up a beer  And you say get over here and play a video game   […]   I say you the bestest  Lean in for a big kiss, put his favorite perfume on  Go play your video game

quote.citation: 2013 August 10, Schumpeter, “Cronies and capitols”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8848:
quote.text: Policing the relationship between government and business in a free society is difficult. […] Governments have to find the best people to fill important jobs: there is a limited supply of people who understand the financial system, for example. But governments must also remember that businesses are self-interested actors who will try to rig the system for their own benefit.

definitions.definition: superlative form of well: most well

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book IX”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC, lines 867–869:
quote.text: Out of my ſight, thou Serpent, that name beſt  Befits thee with him leagu'd, thy ſelf as falſe  And hateful;

quote.citation: 1671, John Milton, “Samson Agonistes, […].”, in Paradise Regain’d. A Poem. In IV Books. To which is Added, Samson Agonistes, London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for John Starkey […], →OCLC, page 65, line 1072:
quote.text: But had we beſt retire, I ſee a ſtorm?

quote.citation: 1797–1798 (date written), [Samuel Taylor Coleridge], “The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere”, in Lyrical Ballads, with a Few Other Poems, London:  […]  J[ohn] & A[rthur] Arch, […], published 1798, →OCLC:
quote.text: He prayeth best, who loveth best / All things both great and small.

quote.citation: 1907 August, Robert W[illiam] Chambers, chapter VIII, in The Younger Set, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: At her invitation he outlined for her the succeeding chapters with terse military accuracy ; and what she liked best and best understood was avoidance of that false modesty which condescends, turning technicality into pabulum.

A popular aphorism says it best: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.

definitions.definition: To the most advantage; with the most success, cause, profit, benefit, or propriety.

quote.citation: 1854, Arthur Pendennis [pseudonym; William Makepeace Thackeray], The Newcomes: Memoirs of a Most Respectable Family, volume (please specify |volume=I or II), London: Bradbury and Evans, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Had I not best go to her?

definitions.definition: (uncountable) The supreme effort one can make, or has made.

quote.citation: 2011 September 28, Tom Rostance, “Arsenal 2 - 1 Olympiakos”, in BBC Sport‎[1]:
quote.text: Home defender Per Mertesacker had to be at his best to stop a dangerous cross from Vassilis Torossidis reaching Djebbour, but moments later Arsenal doubled their lead through Santos.

definitions.definition: (countable) The person (or persons; or thing or things) that is (are) most excellent.

quote.citation: 1994, Otis L. Guernsey, Jeffrey Sweet, The Best Plays of 1993-1994, page vii:
quote.text: Mel Gussow reviews the bests of off off Broadway
But in true Cincinnati style, the bests consistently outnumber the worsts.

quote.citation: 2011, G. Edward Evans, Sheila S. Intner, Jean Riddle Weihs, Introduction to Technical Services, page 149:
quote.text: There are the bests for each institution, the bests for coalitions, and, of course, the bests for the group as a whole.

quote.citation: 2013, Jesse Jose, Collections Of My Best And Most-Hated, "A Cup O' Kapeng Barako" Writings, page 209:
quote.text: If he's one of the bests, he should be fighting the bests, NOT the pipitsugins.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To surpass in skill or achievement.

quote.citation: 1944 July and August, Charles E. Lee, “The "City of Truro"”, in Railway Magazine, pages 201–202:
quote.text: The Norddeutscher Lloyd steamship Kronprinz Wilhelm left New York on May 3 [1904], at 3.10 p.m. and reached Plymouth Sound on May 9 at 8 a.m. This was then a very fast crossing of the Atlantic, but it was not the record. The same ship had held the "Blue Riband" in 1902, but had been slightly bested by the Kaiser Wilhelm II, a larger vessel of the same line, in 1903, and that stood as the record until the Cunard Line secured the honours in 1909 with the Mauretania and held them for an unbroken period of 20 years.

quote.citation: 2010, T. William Phillips, Restless Heart, page 16:
quote.text: "You did not win because I was sloppy. You bested me, Uncle. I've never seen you fight like that before.”

quote.citation: 1935, Edward Joseph O'Brien, John Cournos, editors, The Best British Short Stories of 1935, page 37:
quote.text: 'We best be going,' she said, looking at the clock.

quote.citation: 2010, Mary B. Morrison, Somebody's Gotta Be On Top:
quote.text: Brother, you best be gone when I return.
